title: Research Bite #79: When and How to Use Visuals Effectively: A Meta-Analysis of Dual Coding in the Classroom
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's Research Bite breaks down a meta-analysis from Ambition Institute of 56 randomised classroom experiments, covering 189 results from 6,675 pupils, on whether adding visuals to spoken or written explanations helps learning. Visuals had a moderate positive effect, much larger for secondary than primary pupils and larger in whole-class teaching than in small groups. Effects were strongest when the visual was explicitly linked to the explanation, content was chunked and irrelevant details were removed. Barton turns these into classroom implications such as talking through the visual as you point to it, stripping decoration, pausing between chunks and being wary of asking pupils to copy or label diagrams. The benefits had faded in studies that tested pupils two or more weeks later, so teachers should plan to revisit the visual. He also notes that most studies were one-off lessons run by researchers.
points: Across 56 randomised school experiments, visuals had a moderate positive effect on learning, with secondary pupils gaining over three times as much as primary pupils.
Signalling, meaning pointing to the visual and talking it through, looked the most powerful design choice and more than doubled the effect.
Decorative or irrelevant details shrank the benefit and may even harm learning, so slides should include only images that help explain the content.
Eight of 16 studies that had pupils copy, label or manipulate visuals found negative effects, so teachers should be cautious about such tasks.
Benefits disappeared in studies testing two or more weeks later, so visuals need to be revisited in later lessons.
quotes: A team at Ambition Institute pooled 56 randomised experiments, all run in real schools, to test whether adding visuals such as pictures and diagrams to spoken or written explanations helps pupils learn.

Visuals help pupils learn, and secondary pupils gain the most. Gains were largest when the visual was pointed to and talked through during the explanation, content came in chunks, and anything irrelevant was cut.
Talk through the visual while it is on the board. Of all the design choices tested, signalling looked the most powerful.
The authors expected visuals to work best with small groups or individual pupils. They found the opposite.

This is the big one: when materials contained irrelevant details, the benefit of the visual shrank to the point where it was no longer reliably positive, and the authors warn it may even harm learning.
Segmented content had roughly double the effect of content delivered in one continuous block, and the authors link it especially to helping pupils understand.
In this review, eight of the 16 studies that asked pupils to do something with the visual (copying, filling in a diagram, clicking or dragging on screen) found negative effects.

A diagram in today’s lesson is unlikely to make the learning stick on its own. Bring the same diagram back in later lessons, ask pupils questions about it, and use it to recap before building on the content.
